question.leadin: Identify some of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
question.text: King Nebuchadnezzar ("NEB-uh-kud-NEZZ-ur") of Chaldea ("cal-DEE-uh") built these structures for his wife Amytis ("AM-uh-tis") of Media. They consisted of terraces and irrigation structures that serviced a variety of luscious trees.
question.clue: According to Strabo, an early version of Archimedes' Screw was built for use at this location.

swap.text: Babylonia, a successor state in Mesopotamia, was ruled for a time by this man, whose law code mentioned an "eye for an eye," and is the world's oldest known law code.
swap.clue: This Amorite king went up a mountain to receive a stele from the sun god Shamash that was later discovered in Susa.

question.text: The Sumerians invented textbooks while teaching scribes this Mesopotamian writing system at the eduba. This writing system was designed for reeds to be pressed into clay tablets.
question.clue: Henry Rawlinson studied the Behistun Inscription for insight into this system, which is seen on the oldest complaint tablet.

swap.text: The Code of Hammurabi was issued from this ancient city on the Euphrates[yoo-FRAY-teez]River.
swap.clue: Necho II began a campaign against this city in the Battle of Carchemis, while this city also saw the reign of the Amorite and Kassite dynasties.

question.leadin: Amar-Sin (AA-mar-sin), Shu-Sin (SHOO-sin), and Ibbi-Sin (IB-ee-sin) all succeeded a reformer of this city's Third Dynasty named Shulgi (SHOOL-ghee).
question.text: Name this city near the mouth of the Euphrates (yoo-FRAY-teez), whose Great Ziggurat (ZIG-uh-raht) was later restored by King Nabonidus (NAA-boh-NAI-dus).
question.answerHtml: Ur [or Urim; or Uru; do not accept or prompt on “Uruk”]
question.clue: A king named -Nammu, who founded a dynasty that supplanted Lagash and the Gutians, was succeeded by Shulgi.

swap.leadin: Before becoming ruler of his empire, this man was a cupbearer for Ur-Zababa.
swap.text: Name this ancient ruler who conquered many city-states in Mesopotamia to found the earliest known ancient empire.
swap.answerHtml: Sargon the Great (or Sargon I or Sargon of Akkad)
swap.clue: He appointed his daughter Enheduanna high priestess, and his empire reached its greatest expanse under his grandson Naram-sin.

question.leadin: This ruler's grandmother ordered subjects to support him in the Treaty of Naqia-Zakuto.
question.text: Name this Assyrian king who ordered the destruction of Elam. This ruler's namesake library was constructed in Nineveh.
question.clue: This ruler had to replace the king of Babylon after his brother Shamash-shum-ukin revolted.

swap.leadin: Shalmaneser [shall-mah-NEE-ser] III, a king of this empire, defeated Syrian forces at the Battle of Qarqar ["car-car"].
swap.text: Name this ancient empire. Ashurbanipul [ah-shur-BAH-nih-pall] and Sinsharushkin [sin-shar-ISH-kun] ruled this empire, which was conquered by the Babylonians in 608 B་C་E.
swap.clue: Its army had a special division that was well-versed in sapping and bridge-building techniques, and that division is often referred to as the first military engineers.

question.leadin: The largest remains of one of these structures can be found at Chonga Zanbil, which was built by the Elamites.
question.text: Name these terraced religious buildings. A seven-storied example called the Etemenanki, which was dedicated to the god Marduk, got a reference in Herodotus's histories.
question.clue: Koldewey also found one that he took to be a temple to Marduk, the name of which, Etemenanki, translates as "The Foundation of Heaven and Earth."

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the profession of the scribe.
swap.text: Assyrian or Babylonian scribes probably also produced works in the namesake language of this empire which was commonly spoken throughout Mesopotamia. The founder of this empire, Sargon the Great, won the Battle of Uruk.
swap.clue: Its most famous ruler's life was detailed on the Ebla tablets, and started out as a cup-bearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish.

question.text: This warrior king from the north invaded Sumer beginning around 2340 BCE, creating a unified empire there for the first time.
question.clue: After taking Kish from Lugulzaggesi, he built his empire by extending trade from his capital city throughout to Susa and the Zagros mountains.

swap.leadin: The oldest surviving hymn in the world was written in the language of this civilization.
swap.text: Name this Hurrian kingdom and rival of the Hittites governed from Wassukani. Its king Tusratta wrote a letter to Akhenaten about "The Missing Gold Statues Again."
swap.clue: Based on terms in the Kikkuli horse-training manual, the names of several rulers, and a list of deities found in a treaty, the rulers of this polity are argued to have been Indo-Europeans.

question.text: While conducting excavations in Assyria, Layard found many of these statues of winged human headed bulls, which were often found in pairs at the entrances of buildings. Their male counterparts are called shedu.
question.clue: Several Mesopotamian empires, but most notably the Assyrians, built statues of these protective creatures with a person's face, eagle's wings, and the body of either a bull or a lion.

swap.text: This Sumerian city, which the ancients considered the world's oldest, contained Enki's cult center, the E-Abzu or "House of Deep Waters." Silt accumulated in the Persian Gulf south of this city, where Amar-Sin built a ziggurat.
swap.answerHtml: Eridu [or Irîtu; accept Tell Abu Shahrain; accept Eridu Genesis] (Eridu was once located on the sea, but the silt eventually shifted it over 100 miles inland.)
swap.clue: This Mesopotamian city whose rulers are the first kings mentioned on the Sumerian King List, which is often taken as evidence for this city being the oldest in Sumerian civilization.

question.leadin: Objects such as an axe with a copper and gold handle adorned with a boar attest to the influence of these people's culture in Ugarit.
question.text: Name these people whose namesake language was primarily spoken in the Mitanni kingdom.
question.clue: This ethnic group largely made up the population of the Mitanni Kingdom to the southeast of the Hittite Empire. Kikkuli ("kee-KOO-lee") wrote a horse training manual in this ethnic group's namesake language, which was most closely related to Urartian.

swap.leadin: This ruler is the main character of the Cutha Legend and The Great Revolt, which may have inspired later legends to blame him for Akkad's conquest by the Gutians.
swap.text: Name this ruler of the Akkadian Empire during its territorial peak and the first to proclaim his own divinity. This ruler's namesake "Victory Stele" depicts his victory over the Lullubi people.
swap.clue: This king who ruled during the height of the Akkadian Empire, and erected a notable victory stele boasting of his defeat of the mountain people of Lullubi and depicting himself as a god.

question.leadin: Dominant rulers gradually claimed this title instead of ensi, which kings of Isin and Larsa took as pious stewards of a temple's farmlands.
question.text: Give this Sumerian title that precedes "Anne-Mundu" to identify a "king of the four corners" from Adab, "Zage-Si" to identify a warlord overthrown by Sargon, and "banda" to identify a mythical king of Uruk.

swap.text: The Great Ziggurat was finished by this king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, the son of Ur-Nammu. This king built a 150-mile wall to keep out the Amorites and claimed to have run from Ur to Nippur and back, a total of 200 miles, in a single day.
swap.clue: This king of Ur, the son of Ur-Nammu, completed the construction of Ur's Great Ziggurat. Misinterpretation of the Sumerian writing system led this ruler's name to be originally read as "Dungi."

question.leadin: Answer the following about Larsa, the city which supplanted Isin as the strongest power in lower Mesopotamia before being conquered by Hammurabi.
question.text: Larsa attained independence from Isin under the governor Gungunum, who was of this ethnicity. Hammurabi belonged to this ethnicity, whose members ruled Babylon before the Kassites and Elamites.
question.clue: This Semitic people who established the cities of Ebla and Mari while usurping cities like Kish and Eshnunna. The most famous member of this people conquered Larsa from Rim-Sin I and also instituted a draconian law code demanding "an eye for an eye."

swap.text: Michael Witzel has argued that the BMAC may have left linguistic traces in Sanskrit, Avestan, and the language of this kingdom. This kingdom's elites spoke an Indo-Iranian language and ruled from the city of Washukanni.
